text:
Protosnap’s Methods


1 2 3 4 5





Stable Diffusion model trained specifically on cuneiform images for deep image understanding (SD)
This allows recognition of wedge impressions even with varying lighting, damage, and material textures
Deep diffusion features are used to find matches between prototype images (cuneiform fonts) and sign samples (“best buddy correspondences”)
Two-step alignment

Global alignment: roughly positions the prototype over the photo
Local refinement: adjusts each wedge to its precise location on the tablet

Match each prototype wedge to its impression in the tablet photo

title: Measuring Scribal Literacy Through Quantitative Analysis
text:
What is Geometric-Morphometrics (GMM)?


1 2 3 4 5





GMM quantitatively analyzes shape using geometric coordinates (not just measurements)
Shape is captured by placing landmarks (homologous points) on each object
Variables are the cartesian coordinates of these landmarks
Size is not included; the focus is on shape only
Results can be visualized as images
Several analysis variants exist (e.g., EDMA)

title: Measuring Scribal Literacy Through Quantitative Analysis

GMM Workflow & Procrustes Superimposition


1 2 3 4 5





Collect landmark data (same number & order for all shapes)
Perform Procrustes superimposition to standardize shapes
Analyze shape similarity and difference
Procrustes superimposition:

Removes size, translation, and rotation
Aligns all shapes to a common coordinate system
Also called Procrustes analysis, GPA, or least squares fitting
Enables direct comparison of shape differences

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Method: a reference space of traditions
text:
Method: a reference space of traditions



Corpus: TLHdig 0.3 XML, 23,526 manuscripts, 1.24 M words, converted following Yavasan and Gordin, From Clay to Code (ALP 2025)
Two feature spaces

word tf-idf (normalised forms) for content
sign n-grams (1–3 signs within a word) for orthography

Traditions as centroids: each tradition is the mean of its manuscripts
Assignment: a fragment goes to its most similar centroid, or to none if the lead over the runner-up is too small (open set)


Reference traditions, each defined by the study that argued for it


Hurrian festivals (StBoT 73): Kizzuwatna–Lower Land; Syro-Mesopotamia, incl. CTH 701; Mixed
Luwian and Palaic festivals (HFR modules): Ištanuwa and Lallupiya; Ḫuwaššanna; Palaic
Kizzuwatna rituals (Miller 2004): CTH 471–499 + 404
Western (Arzawa) rituals (colophons; Bawanypeck 2005)
Luwian rituals of Puriyanni and Kuwattalla (StBoT 72)
Hattian cult layer (Klinger 1996)


Orphans (CTH 470 + EBo) are never part of the reference.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
Validation: leave one manuscript out


Every manuscript of 17+ words is removed in turn and reassigned. Baselines: always guessing the largest class, and the same procedure with shuffled labels (200 permutations).


Historical groups: 72% over 6 classes, against a 23% majority baseline. CTH 670/701/832 as in the abstract: 89%, but the majority baseline is already 78% (CTH 670 dominates), so it shows little. This is why the reference space moved to historical groups.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: How small can an orphan be?
text:
How small can an orphan be?


Long manuscripts are cut into random windows of k words and reassigned. Words and signs perform alike, and signs are slightly better from about 8 words up.


3 words: about 53%; 10 words: about 68%; 40 words: about 79%, against a chance level of 10% (10 traditions). This curve sets the abstention rule used for the orphans.

Remove all logograms (Sumero- and Akkadograms)

word tf-idf: 82% → 76%
sign n-grams: 84% → 81%

The signal survives without the cultic logographic vocabulary.

Script date (MS vs NS)

inside CTH 701 the method does not predict script date above the majority baseline (73% vs 83%)
neither do the orthographic rates (79% vs 83%)

So the groupings are not script-date clusters.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Where do CTH 470 and EBo fragments go?
text:
Where do CTH 470 and EBo fragments go?


Orphans with 5+ legible words. A fragment is assigned only when its lead over the runner-up passes the margin at which the window test reaches 80% precision (0.018; bootstrap 90% interval 0.018–0.019).


847 of 2,026 orphans assigned: Kizzuwatna rituals 513, Hattian 130, Kizzuwatna–Lower Land 68, Syro-Mesopotamia 60, Puriyanni/Kuwattalla 21, Mixed 21, Ḫuwaššanna 12, Arzawa 11, Ištanuwa/Lallupiya 8, Palaic 3.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
QTM: orphans as low-coverage witnesses

Each tradition is treated as an archetype, approximated by its most characteristic terms
Each orphan is a witness that attests a small part of it
Coverage asks how much of each archetype the orphans collectively attest
Archetypes with little coverage are transmissions we only see through the reference corpus. High coverage from orphans alone points to traditions that circulated widely in fragments.


E6, first pass: the Kizzuwatna rituals (574 assigned orphans) and the Hattian layer (142) attest 100% and 98% of their 200 core terms, the Hurrian festival groups 66–93%, and the small groups (Luwian, Palaic, Arzawa, Puriyanni/Kuwattalla; 4–22 orphans each) 34–67%. Coverage grows with the number of orphans, so these numbers still need rarefaction (equal orphan counts per tradition) before they can be compared.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
Limits and next steps

Normalisation: TLHdig trans forms are uneven across editors, and broken words are dropped
Preservation bias: short fragments over-represent formulaic lines
Open set: the genre gate needs more outside classes, and the two small ritual traditions (Arzawa, Puriyanni/Kuwattalla) need more manuscripts before they can be trusted
Function, not tradition: festival manuscripts differ by use (Burgin 2019, StBoT 65), which word profiles may pick up
Joins: an orphan placed near a known manuscript is a candidate join to check on the tablet
Palaeography: link to sign-shape measurement (DANES 2025) for the same fragments
Common material: a quarter of the assigned orphans rest mostly on features every tradition shares; a rule to flag them is the next step
Philological check: worked examples (top-ranked orphans per tradition) for colleagues to verify

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Word classes: function words and verbs are not where tradition lives
text:
Word classes: function words and verbs are not where tradition lives


The six categories of StBoT 73 Table 4. Each class alone (blue) and everything except it (orange); word forms, leave one manuscript out.


Removing function words, verbs or agents costs almost nothing (82% → 80–82%): these classes are shared across traditions, a common scribal and syntactic layer. Alone they still reach 54–57% against 30%, so formulae differ between traditions, but less than realia (70%) or foreign words (83%). Removing realia costs the most (82% → 75%), then foreign words (78%). Inside CTH 701 the Hurrian recitations carry the subgroups: removing them costs the most (51% → 47%), yet 47% is still twice the majority baseline (21%).

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
Validation with literature-defined traditions


Kizzuwatna rituals = CTH 471–499 + 404 (Miller 2004); Western (Arzawa) = CTH 394, 402, 406, 410 (colophon: from Arzawa or Ḫapalla) and 425, 433 (augurs; Bawanypeck 2005); Luwian rituals of Puriyanni and Kuwattalla = CTH 758–763 (Yakubovich and Mouton 2023); Hattian cult layer = Klinger 1996 (from the Konkordanz citations of StBoT 37); the three Hurrian festival groups of StBoT 73; StBoT 73’s Luwian group split as the HFR edition modules split it (Ištanuwa and Lallupiya: CTH 665, 771–773; Ḫuwaššanna: 690–694), plus HFR’s Palaic festivals (750–754). CTH 390–469 texts claimed by no study (including the Ambazzi rituals) and the CTH 500 fragment collection leave the reference and are placed like orphans.


84% over 10 traditions against 30% majority, up from 72% with the CTH-range controls. Hattian 95%, Kizzuwatna 92%, Ḫuwaššanna 91%, Ištanuwa/Lallupiya 84%, Palaic 82%. The two small ritual groups are weakest: Arzawa 64% (11 manuscripts long enough to test), Puriyanni/Kuwattalla 40% (10). The HFR split holds: StBoT 73’s single Luwian group hides two cult traditions that the texts keep apart. CTH 500 (“fragments of Kizzuwatna rituals”, 235 manuscripts) is a fragment collection, not a composition, and it pulled every generic ritual into Kizzuwatna. Placed like orphans, only 54 of its 128 assigned fragments go to the Kizzuwatna rituals; 73 go to the Hurrian festival groups. That fits HFR, which counts CTH 500 among its festival texts. The CTH 390–469 residue still goes mostly to Kizzuwatna (152 of 186 assigned), 13 to Puriyanni/Kuwattalla: the only large ritual class wins on genre, not on origin. The Ambazzi manuscripts go 3 to Kizzuwatna, 3 unassigned, none to Arzawa.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Test against the HFR festival modules
text:
Test against the HFR festival modules


The Luwian group split as the HFR editions split it: Luwian festivals of Ištanuwa and Lallupiya (CTH 665, 771–773, as listed by HFR) and Ḫuwaššanna (CTH 690–694); Palaic festivals (CTH 750–754) added. Other groups as on the previous slide.


84% over 9 groups (30% majority). The HFR modules hold up: Ḫuwaššanna 91%, Ištanuwa/Lallupiya 84%, Palaic 82%. So StBoT 73’s single “Luwian cult centres” group hides two cult traditions that the texts themselves keep apart. Only the module lists HFR publishes are used; its planned modules (Nerik, Zippalanda, KI.LAM …) give no CTH lists yet.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Does a fragment fit any known tradition?
text:
Does a fragment fit any known tradition?


Texts of genres outside the reference (Laroche’s genre blocks; cult inventories, Cammarosano 2021; Luwian rituals of Taurisa, CTH 764–766), cut to 10-word windows. Orange: share placed in a tradition anyway. Blue: share recognised as outside when the outside genres become classes of their own.


The margin rule alone still places 12–33% of windows of other genres, and 60% of festivals of other traditions. A genre gate recognises 87–97% of the other genres and 62% of the other festivals, at the cost of sending 22% of reference windows away. Applied to the orphans: 212 of 2,026 are closer to an outside genre than to any tradition, beyond the margin; 73 of them had been assigned (Hattian-layer orphans that look like festivals of other traditions, 21; Kizzuwatna orphans that look like myths, 16, or instructions, 10). These are candidates for re-filing.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Leave one composition out: are the scholarly groups recovered?
text:
Leave one composition out: are the scholarly groups recovered?


Each CTH number is removed with all its manuscripts and placed against the traditions built from the rest, so no copy or duplicate of the same composition can help.


57 of 78 compositions (73%) land in their scholarly tradition. Confirmed where a tradition has many compositions: Hattian layer 25 of 25, Ḫuwaššanna 5 of 5, Kizzuwatna rituals 16 of 18. StBoT 73’s three Hurrian festival groups hold only 7 of 17: CTH 701 goes to the Kizzuwatna rituals, 698 to Kizzuwatna–Lower Land. Palaic festivals: 3 of 5 go to the Hattian layer. The two small ritual groups rest on one large composition each (433 augurs, 760 Kuwattalla); held out, both go to the Kizzuwatna rituals.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: A contested attribution: the Ambazzi rituals
text:
A contested attribution: the Ambazzi rituals






The six Ambazzi manuscripts (CTH 391, 429, 463), pooled, rank the western (Arzawa) group 8th of 10; their lead is what random unassigned rituals get (p = 0.18)
None of the 20 most distinctive western words occurs in them except É: no kurša- “hunting bag”, KAL, MUŠEN.DÙ “augur”, TU₇, paimi, pattar
Their own words (ḫaršialli, aki, petaz) occur in at most 3% of any tradition’s manuscripts
Nearest is Kizzuwatna (5 of 6), but no more than for any unassigned ritual (p = 0.66): a generic ritual, not a member of a defined tradition




The method tested against a scholarly attribution. Christiansen 2006 shows Luwian influence; grouping Ambazzi with the western rituals was our own first literature grouping, and the method does not support it. Caveat: the western group is small and dominated by the augur rituals (CTH 433). Files: E10b_contested_fit.csv, E10c_signatures_in_contested.csv, E10c_contested_own_words.csv.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: What a placement rests on: similarity is not the decision
text:
What a placement rests on: similarity is not the decision


The score is a cosine, so it splits exactly over the features, and each feature over the words it occurs in (word category) and its layer (word form, syllabic or logographic signs). Correctly placed reference manuscripts, leave one out.


Similarity to a tradition is 47% common material (nu, the signs a, i); the decision (lead over the runner-up) only 11%, because what all traditions share cancels
Delete the 100 most frequent words (44% of all words): accuracy 84% → 83%


This answers the playground observation that “nu” carries weight: it carries similarity, which is what the playground shades, but not the decision. The 25 most frequent forms are 15% of the similarity and 2% of the decision. What decides, by category: nouns and realia 33%, agents and deities 32%, foreign words 13%, verbs 11%, function words 9%. By layer: syllabic signs 51%, logographic signs 32%, word forms 17%. Caveat: a syllabic sign n-gram carries the word as well as its spelling (ḫu-wa-aš is Ḫuwaššanna). The spelling layer of the layers slide isolates the spelling choice: it adds about one point. Files: run_attribution.py, E11_report.json, E11a_category_by_layer.csv, E11b_top_features.csv.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: When the decision rests on common material, distrust it
text:
When the decision rests on common material, distrust it


Windows of 5, 10 and 20 words from held-out reference manuscripts, placed with the abstention margin. Common features: attested in at least a quarter of the reference manuscripts.


Short windows placed mostly on common features are right 54–62% of the time, against 76–84% for the rest. For short fragments the worry about nu is right: in orphans of 5–10 words common features carry 28% of the decision. 227 of the 847 assigned orphans rest mostly on common features; they are flagged in E11a_orphan_decomposition.csv as weaker placements. Refitting without function words, 651 of the 847 assigned orphans keep their tradition, 5 move and 191 fall below the margin (E11e).

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
What would a philologist say?


The clues point in more than one direction

The Old Woman and the physician are the practitioners of the Kizzuwatna rituals (Miller 2004), the largest ritual tradition
“The tongue of the multitude” belongs to the Luwian purification rituals of the Lower Land: the Great Ritual of Kuwattalla (CTH 760; Mouton and Yakubovich 2019) and the rituals of Tunnawiya (CTH 409)
Tunnawiya and Kuwattalla were compared already by Laroche (1955); Mouton places both in the Lower Land, Kuwattalla as the more “Hurrianized”; Miller (2004: 255–58) keeps CTH 409 apart from the Kizzuwatna rituals


What the method can add

Which tradition the whole fragment resembles, and by how much
Which words carry that decision
Which manuscripts are closest, as places to look for a parallel or a join
Whether the answer is strong enough to state, or the fragment should stay unplaced



The scholarly literature gives candidates, not an answer: three traditions are plausible for this fragment. References: Laroche 1955 (RHA 13/57); Miller 2004 (StBoT 46): 255–58; Mouton 2015; Mouton and Yakubovich 2019 (BSOAS 82/2); Goetze and Sturtevant 1938; Hutter 1988. Check page references before the talk. We return to KBo 41.22 in section 6.

The CTH is a catalogue of compositions. When the composition is unknown, a fragment goes to a genre bin
The bins are filing decisions, not traditions: CTH 500 is a running list; CTH 390–469 holds named rituals that no study has grouped
Traditional assignment needs a parallel passage, which is exactly what these fragments lack
The question: can the content and spelling of a fragment point to its tradition, and when should we say we do not know?



Numbers from stats_corpus.py (corpus_stats.json, laroche_bins). The EBo fragments, digitised in TLHdig 0.3 (May 2026), are filed mostly under CTH 832 and 670, which are themselves bins. The median of 4 words for CTH 832 and EBo is the hard constraint for everything that follows.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: How this approach treats the bins
text:
How this approach treats the bins

Build a reference from traditions that published studies define, not from CTH ranges
Place each fragment with the tradition it resembles most, or abstain when the lead over the runner-up is small
Show the evidence: every placement splits into the words and sign sequences that carry it
Test the bins themselves: CTH 500 and the CTH 390–469 residue are placed like orphans, not used as reference
Hand the result back to philology: a placement is a hypothesis, with the nearest manuscripts as candidate parallels and joins

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: What we mean by a tradition
text:
What we mean by a tradition



A tradition is a group of compositions that a published study ties together by an external criterion:

a place of origin (“from Kizzuwatna”, “from Arzawa”)
a named practitioner (Puriyanni, Kuwattalla)
a cult centre or deity (Ištanuwa, Ḫuwaššanna)
a language layer (Hattian, Palaic)

The criterion is not the vocabulary we measure, so the test is not circular
Laroche’s CTH numbers are the addresses: each tradition is a list of CTH numbers taken from its defining study


An archetype is the tradition’s profile in the data: the mean of its manuscripts’ word and sign frequencies.
An orphan is a fragment that no edition has placed in a composition (CTH 470 and the EBo fragments). Orphans are never part of the reference.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
The pipeline


Corpus: TLHdig 0.3 XML, 23,526 manuscripts, 1.24 M words, converted following Yavasan and Gordin, From Clay to Code (ALP 2025). Two feature spaces: word tf-idf (what is written) and sign n-grams of 1–3 signs within a word (how it is written). Each tradition is the centroid of its manuscripts; a fragment goes to its nearest centroid only if its lead over the runner-up passes the margin (0.018). Figure from the paper (paper/figures/pipeline.tex), built from the same results files.

An audit of the rules found seven systematic errors (prepositions joined to nouns, possessive suffixes, theophoric names, GAL as an agent …); fixing them changed 9.3% of the words, and every experiment was rerun
Correcting by hand: a review sheet of the most frequent forms and a corrections file that every run applies (review_wordclass.py)
Known limits: “realia” includes adjectives and place names; 10.5% unknown, half of them broken words; syllabic Akkadian ana, ša have no analysis; participles count as verbs
A blind sample of 180 words (60 per level) is ready for a philologist’s check




The class results (word classes and decision shares) should be read with this confidence in mind; removing a whole class changes accuracy by at most 7 points (E8), so a few per cent of misclassified words cannot drive them. Rule changes before and after the audit: results/wordclass_rule_changes.csv.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Do the traditions hold? Leave one manuscript out
text:
Do the traditions hold? Leave one manuscript out


Every manuscript of 17+ words is removed in turn and placed against the traditions built from the rest. Baselines: always guessing the largest tradition, and the same procedure with shuffled labels (200 permutations).


84% over 10 traditions against a 30% majority baseline (p = 0.005). With Laroche’s CTH ranges as classes, 72% against 23%. By tradition: Hattian 95%, Ḫuwaššanna 93%, Kizzuwatna rituals 92%, Ištanuwa/Lallupiya 83%, Palaic 82%, Kizzuwatna–Lower Land 82%, Syro-Mesopotamia 68%, Mixed 68%, Arzawa 64% (11 manuscripts), Puriyanni/Kuwattalla 40% (10).

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: How small can a fragment be?
text:
How small can a fragment be?


Long manuscripts are cut into random windows of k words and placed. The abstention margin (0.018) is set where placed windows are right 80% of the time.


3 words: 50%; 10 words: 65%; 40 words: 78%, against a chance level of 10%. Above the margin, 80% of placed windows are right and 66% of windows are placed.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: Testing the hint: is Tunnawiya part of the Kuwattalla tradition?
text:
Testing the hint: is Tunnawiya part of the Kuwattalla tradition?






The 32 Tunnawiya manuscripts (CTH 409), pooled, are nearest to Puriyanni and Kuwattalla, just ahead of the Kizzuwatna rituals (+0.007)
Random unassigned rituals fall far below Kuwattalla (−0.29); Tunnawiya does not: p = 0.0005
Random rituals lean toward Kizzuwatna (+0.08); Tunnawiya does not: it is less Kizzuwatna-like than a generic ritual
One by one, the manuscripts split 14 Kuwattalla, 14 Kizzuwatna




Same test as for Ambazzi (run_hypotheses.py –cths 409, results/tlhdig03_literature/tunnawiya/). This fits Laroche’s comparison and Mouton’s Lower Land setting, and Miller’s separation of CTH 409 from the Kizzuwatna rituals. The per-manuscript split is a caution: short manuscripts of either tradition look alike. A fragment led us to a statement about a whole composition.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
text:
Testing Laroche’s bins


CTH 500, “fragments of Kizzuwatna rituals”

132 of 242 manuscripts placed
only 53 go to the Kizzuwatna rituals; 78 go to the Hurrian festival groups (32 Syro-Mesopotamia, 31 Kizzuwatna–Lower Land, 15 Mixed)
Fits HFR, which counts CTH 500 among its festival texts


CTH 390–469, rituals no study groups

169 of 314 manuscripts placed
138 to the Kizzuwatna rituals, 15 Hattian, 12 Puriyanni/Kuwattalla
The largest ritual tradition attracts generic ritual language: a Kizzuwatna placement of a ritual fragment is the weakest kind

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: QTM: orphans as witnesses of archetypes
text:
QTM: orphans as witnesses of archetypes

Each tradition is an archetype, approximated by its 200 most characteristic terms
Each orphan is a witness that attests a small part of it
Coverage: how much of each archetype the orphans placed in it attest together
Kizzuwatna rituals 100% (513 orphans), Hattian 98% (130), Kizzuwatna–Lower Land 94% (68), Syro-Mesopotamia 92% (60); the small traditions 28–68% (3–21 orphans)


Coverage grows with the number of orphans, so these numbers need rarefaction (equal orphan counts per tradition) before they can be compared. Archetypes with little coverage are transmissions we see only through the reference corpus.

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: What we learned about the traditions
text:
What we learned about the traditions


Coherent, composition by composition: the Hattian cult layer (25 of 25 compositions), Ḫuwaššanna (5 of 5), the Kizzuwatna rituals (16 of 18)
StBoT 73’s Luwian group is two traditions: Ištanuwa and Lallupiya vs Ḫuwaššanna, as the HFR edition splits them
The three Hurrian festival groups are a continuum: held together by their large compositions (7 of 17 recovered); CTH 500 belongs with them more than with the Kizzuwatna rituals
Palaic festivals lean to the Hattian layer (3 of 5 compositions): a shared Old Anatolian cult layer
Traditions are marked by different things: deities and cult personnel (Ḫuwaššanna, Palaic), ritual materials (Kizzuwatna), language layer (Hattian, Palaic), formulae (Mixed, Syro-Mesopotamia)
Spelling marks the copying line, not the tradition
Two scholarly questions answered by the data: the Ambazzi rituals are not western; Tunnawiya goes with Kuwattalla and away from Kizzuwatna

title: Orphans and Archetypes
section: What the method adds, and its limits
text:
What the method adds, and its limits


Adds

A placement or an honest abstention for each fragment, with its strength
The words behind each placement, to check by eye
Nearest manuscripts as candidate parallels and joins
Tests of scholarly groupings against random rituals


Limits

Short fragments: 10 words are right 65% of the time
Placements resting on common material are weak (227 of 847)
Small traditions (Arzawa, Puriyanni/Kuwattalla: 10–11 manuscripts) cannot yet be trusted
Word categories are rule-based and 12% low-confidence; a philologist’s audit is pending
Festival manuscripts differ by use (Burgin 2019), which word profiles may pick up



Next steps: rarefied coverage; the 180-word audit; sign-shape measurement (DANES 2025) for the same fragments; worked examples per tradition for colleagues to verify.
